items.readable_text:
Content:
Derivatives naturally occur in many real-world situations, so it's essential to know their units of measurement. The key is to remember that the derivative represents a rate of change.

Content:
For instance, suppose that the temperature of a pizza [MATH: t] minutes after coming out of a hot oven is [MATH: T(t)] degrees Fahrenheit. What are the units of [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}T}{\textrm{d}t}?]

Content:
First, we have that the temperature [MATH: T(t)] is measured in degrees Fahrenheit and the time [MATH: t] is measured in minutes.

Content:
[MATH: T(t):|degrees Fahrenheit; t:|minutes]

Content:
The derivative [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}\color{black}T}{\textrm{d}\color{black}t}] measures a change in [MATH: {\color{black}T}] over a change in [MATH: {\color{black}t}.] So, it represents a ratio of the units:
[MATH: (dT)/(dt):|(degrees Fahrenheit)/(minutes)]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}\color{black}T}{\textrm{d}\color{black}t}] is measured in "degrees Fahrenheit per minute", or [MATH: ^\circ \textrm F / \textrm {min}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We have that the height [MATH: r(t)] is measured in meters and the time is measured in seconds. [MATH: r(t):|meters; t:|seconds]

The derivative [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}] measures a change in [MATH: r(t)] over a change in [MATH: t.] So, it represents a ratio of the units: [MATH: (dr)/(dt):|(meters)/(seconds)]

Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}] is measured in "meters per second".

sections.normalized_html: Consider a spherical balloon with radius [MATH: r.] As the balloon loses air, its volume [MATH: V] decreases. What is the best interpretation of [MATH: V'(r)?]
sections.readable_text:
Consider a spherical balloon with radius [MATH: r.] As the balloon loses air, its volume [MATH: V] decreases. What is the best interpretation of [MATH: V'(r)?]

[IMG: /graphics/fe67280942729a8d2c75f11df00d3dde]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The function [MATH: V(r)] gives the volume of a sphere with radius [MATH: r.] So [MATH: V'(r) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}V}{\textrm{d}r} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }V}{\textrm{Change in }r}.]

Therefore, [MATH: V'(r)] is the rate at which the volume changes as the radius changes.

sections.normalized_html: The function [MATH: B(s)] models a school's budget, in dollars, given the average number of students [MATH: s] in each grade. What is the best interpretation of [MATH: B'(30)=2\,000?]
sections.readable_text: The function [MATH: B(s)] models a school's budget, in dollars, given the average number of students [MATH: s] in each grade. What is the best interpretation of [MATH: B'(30)=2\,000?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The function [MATH: B'(s)] represents the rate at which the budget is changing at the moment when the school has an average of exactly [MATH: s] students in each grade.

Therefore, [MATH: B'(30) = 2\,000] means:

When the school has an average of [MATH: 30] students in each grade, its budget is increasing at a rate of [MATH: 2\,000] dollars per student.

items.title: Determining a Rate of Change

sections.normalized_html:
On a particular day, the rate [MATH: E] at which tourists enter a small country can be modeled as [MATH: E(t) = 50\cdot 3^{0.2t}] tourists per hour, where [MATH: t] is the time, in hours, after midnight. The rate at which tourists leave the country can be modeled as [MATH: L(t)=100\cdot 2^{0.2t}] tourists per hour, where [MATH: t] is also the time in hours after midnight.

What is the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}?]
sections.readable_text:

The rate at which tourists leave the country can be modeled as [MATH: L(t)=100\cdot 2^{0.2t}] tourists per hour, where [MATH: t] is also the time in hours after midnight.

What is the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The rate of change of the number of tourists in the country at time [MATH: t] is equal to the entry rate minus the exit rate at time [MATH: t,] that is, [MATH: E(t)-L(t).]

Since [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}] is ten hours after midnight, we have [MATH: t=10.] Substituting [MATH: t=10,] the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}] is [MATH: E(10) − L(10)|= 50 ⋅ 3^{0.2(10)} − 100 ⋅ 2^{0.2(10)}; = 450 − 400; = 50.]

Therefore, the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}] is [MATH: 50] tourists per hour.

sections.normalized_html:
The function [MATH: N(t)] gives the number of people inside the convention [MATH: t] minutes after opening. Then, [MATH: N'(t) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}N(t)}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }N}{\textrm{Change in }t}.] Thus, [MATH: N'(t)] gives the rate at which the number of people inside the convention changes [MATH: t] minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the convention at time [MATH: t] by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time [MATH: t.] That is, [MATH: N'(t) = E(t) - L(t).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Derivatives naturally occur in many real-world situations, so it's essential to know their units of measurement. The key is to remember that the derivative represents a rate of change.

Content:
For instance, suppose that the temperature of a pizza [MATH: t] minutes after coming out of a hot oven is [MATH: T(t)] degrees Fahrenheit. What are the units of [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}T}{\textrm{d}t}?]

Content:
First, we have that the temperature [MATH: T(t)] is measured in degrees Fahrenheit and the time [MATH: t] is measured in minutes.

Content:
[MATH: T(t):|degrees Fahrenheit; t:|minutes]

Content:
The derivative [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}\color{black}T}{\textrm{d}\color{black}t}] measures a change in [MATH: {\color{black}T}] over a change in [MATH: {\color{black}t}.] So, it represents a ratio of the units:
[MATH: (dT)/(dt):|(degrees Fahrenheit)/(minutes)]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}\color{black}T}{\textrm{d}\color{black}t}] is measured in "degrees Fahrenheit per minute", or [MATH: ^\circ \textrm F / \textrm {min}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining the Units of a Derivative

Example Prompt:
A rocket is at a distance of [MATH: r(t)] meters from the ground [MATH: t] seconds after it is launched. What are the units of [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have that the height [MATH: r(t)] is measured in meters and the time is measured in seconds.
[MATH: r(t):|meters; t:|seconds]

The derivative [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}] measures a change in [MATH: r(t)] over a change in [MATH: t.] So, it represents a ratio of the units:
[MATH: (dr)/(dt):|(meters)/(seconds)]

Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}] is measured in "meters per second".

---

Item 5 — Example: Interpreting the Derivative of a Function

Example Prompt:
Consider a spherical balloon with radius [MATH: r.] As the balloon loses air, its volume [MATH: V] decreases. What is the best interpretation of [MATH: V'(r)?]

[IMG: /graphics/fe67280942729a8d2c75f11df00d3dde]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The function [MATH: V(r)] gives the volume of a sphere with radius [MATH: r.] So
[MATH: V'(r) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}V}{\textrm{d}r} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }V}{\textrm{Change in }r}.]

Therefore, [MATH: V'(r)] is the rate at which the volume changes as the radius changes.

The function [MATH: B'(s)] represents the rate at which the budget is changing at the moment when the school has an average of exactly [MATH: s] students in each grade.

> When the school has an average of [MATH: 30] students in each grade, its budget is increasing at a rate of [MATH: 2\,000] dollars per student.

Item 11 — Example: Determining a Rate of Change

Example Prompt:
On a particular day, the rate [MATH: E] at which tourists enter a small country can be modeled as [MATH: E(t) = 50\cdot 3^{0.2t}] tourists per hour, where [MATH: t] is the time, in hours, after midnight. The rate at which tourists leave the country can be modeled as [MATH: L(t)=100\cdot 2^{0.2t}] tourists per hour, where [MATH: t] is also the time in hours after midnight.

What is the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The rate of change of the number of tourists in the country at time [MATH: t] is equal to the entry rate minus the exit rate at time [MATH: t,] that is,
[MATH: E(t)-L(t).]

Since [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}] is ten hours after midnight, we have [MATH: t=10.] Substituting [MATH: t=10,] the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}] is
[MATH: E(10) − L(10)|= 50 ⋅ 3^{0.2(10)} − 100 ⋅ 2^{0.2(10)}; = 450 − 400; = 50.]

Therefore, the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at [MATH: 10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}] is [MATH: 50] tourists per hour.

---
